Come down to ~ boil down to

\"For real? This is (not a logical) decision at all! Just think about it one more time\"
The correct word is \"illogical\" (for example: \"This is an extremely illogical decision you\'ve ever taken\")
\"Is this sentence grammatically correct?\nIt looks a bit too weird.\"
\"To not seem rude people can minimize such words like \'too\' into \'a bit too.\'\"
\"I want you to come over so that we have so much fun and celebrate Halloween\"
\"I\'d like you to come along with me there tonight. Do you have any plans for today?\"
\"I\'ve been going through a lot: I\'ve got exams coming up and I\'m studying so that I could pass them\"
\"I watch a lotta English video lessons on YouTube so that my English skills are better\"
The third sentence is incorrect because we need to use Present Simple when the first part of the sentence has the Present Progressive tense (for example: \"I\'m studying so that I can pass them\")
What does the word \"moving\" mean in this context?\n\"It was a very moving scene\"
Moving - causing strong feelings of sadness or sympathy.
PASSIVE VOICE: Please, choose the correct sentence
This building is repaired right now
This phone is being sold now
The sentence \"This building is repaired right now\" is not correct. You need to use \"is being\" because there is \"right now\" in the end (for example: \"The ceiling is being painted now\").
Is it a correct dialogue?\n\n-Where shall I put this vase? -Put it anyplace -it doesn\'t matter where.
The adverb \"anyplace\" is informal and used mainly in the US. It means \"anywhere\".
\"-Haven\'t you seen my key, Emily? -Sorry, darling, I left it in the flat.\"\nHow would you pronounce the word \'key\'?
A person who cooks well is a good cook.
I\'m making an amazing desert in the kitchen right now.
I\'ve always wanted to be able to cook very well.
DeSert (countable or uncountable) - a large, hot, dry area of land with very few plants.\nDeSsert (countable and uncountable) - sweet food.
TAG QUESTIONS: please, choose the correct sentence for the given statement:
\"Nobody lives in that shabby house, do they?\"
\"Nobody lives in that shabby house, does they?\"
\"Nobody lives in that shabby house, isn\'t it?\"
\"Nobody lives in that shabby house, aren\'t they?\"
The first sentence is correct because \"nobody\" (also \"no one\") means \"they\"; \"they\" comes with \"do\" (for example: \"No one cares, do they?\").
DEPENDENT PREPOSITIONS: please, choose the incorrect sentence
\"I\'d say smiling at strangers is typical of American culture. I think, that\'s so cool!\"
\"My city is covered with snow and it looks so wonderful and charming!\"
\"Oh my gosh, this guy is so cruel to her! Stop him anybody!\"
\"You were so polite for me and I appreciated that!\"
The first and the second sentences are incorrect
The third and the fourth sentences are incorrect
All of the sentences except the fourth one are correct. We need to use the preposition \"to\" (\"___ to someone\") (for example: \"The staff in this store is so polite to customers\").
Choose the WRONG sentence, if any.
Mike and Lisa went to bed very early yesterday because they were exhausted.
Because Mike and Helen were exhausted, they went to bed very early yesterday.
1) In a sentence \'because\' can be both at the beginning and in the middle;\n2) We put a comma after a subordinate clause if \'because\' is at the beginning of a sentence.
Do the \"to bring forward\" and \"to put off\" phrasal verbs mean the same thing?

The \"to bring forward\" and \"to put off\" phrasal verbs do not mean the same. They mean \"to postpone\", but the \"to bring forward\" phrasal verb also means \"to introduce something\" (\"to introduce an idea\").
Complete the dialogue:\n- Jessica, by the way, where ___ last week? - I ___ in Switzerland with my colleagues.
The first and fourth options are correct
The action happened at a definite time in the past. The time is mentioned (\"last week\"). So, we use the Past Simple, not the Present Perfect.
Complete the following dialogue:\n- Mark, how long did it take you to wait ___ a postman? - Alice, you know, it took so long. I waited ___ five hours.

1) With a period of time, \"for\" after \"wait\" is optional (= not necessary, but possible);\n2) BUT! \"to wait FOR someone/something\". In this case, \"for\" after \"wait\" is essential: I waited for the parcel.
\"Unfortunately, Jessica called us to say she would be late at the conference\"
\"John told me he will be at the meeting on time. That\'s great!\"

When there is the Future-in-the-Past tense, \"would\" or \"would be\" are used instead of \"will\" or \"will be\" (for example: \"He said he would go there tomorrow\"). Therefore, the first sentence is correct.
Complete the saying:\nKeep your friends ___ and your enemies ___ .
What does the \"oddball\" slang word mean?\n\"Our new boss is a bit of an oddball, go just look at him\"
The \"oddball\" slang word is a noun that means someone is a weird, unusual, or eccentric person. This word also means something is strange or unusual.
Choose the correct preposition.\nThe trip ended ___ tragedy
The correct preposition is \"in\". We say \"end in tragedy\" when describing a situation that results in a tragic outcome.
Fill in the gap.\nThe painting is just a copy - it\'s not ___.
\"Authentic\" means real or original, not fake, not copied.
This course consists of three parts
This dish contains a lot of salt
He finds his socks in the fridge every Saturday
Lucy found her purse at last
John founded the company last year
1) find - found - found (irregular verb);\n2) found - founded - founded (regular verb).
Complete the dialogue:\n-Max, why didn\'t you call me back yesterday? -Sorry, darling! When I came home, I ___ down on the bed and fell asleep immediately
Complete the dialogue:\n-Alice, you know, these exams are so difficult
Yeah, I understand. Hang in there!
Yeah, I understand. Hang on in there!
1) (idiom) hang in there (UK also \'hang on in there\') - said as a way of telling someone to not give up, despite difficulties.
The collocation \"a jar of wood\" is incorrect. For example, we can say \"a jar of honey\" or \"a piece of wood\", but wood is not typically stored in a jar.
I need to buy a new jeans.
Does the police know the cause of the explosion?
She\'s given me some terrific ideas.
I\'ve recovered completely. I feel terrific.
They did a terrific job painting the house.
1) The correct spelling is \"teRRific\" (double R). Ensure you carefully review the spelling of each word in the options.
PREPOSITIONS: Choose the correct preposition. My cat hissed ___ me, when I stepped on its tail.
Choose the wrong spelling of the word. You\'re not a child anymore! Don\'t be so ___!
Joan wanted to go to a movie but I wasn\'t keen.
They were very keen to start work as soon as possible.
He\'s rather keen a girl in his school.
He\'s rather keen on a girl in his school. In this sentence, \"keen on somebody\" means be very interested in someone.
1) To be in no hurry (to do something);\n2) The opposite of this expression is \"to be in a hurry\" (to do something).
VOCABULARY: We ___ the train because we had woken (up) too late.
Choose the correct form of verb. The eggs were taken from the eagle\'s nest. Police believe they will now ___ out of the country and sold abroad.
Theme: Passive voice. According to the rule \"will be + V3/Ved,\" it must be \"will be smuggled.\"
\"I\'d rather not to say my name in public because I keep myself anonymous\"
\"I had rather not come along with them, they\'re kinda shady and___ weird\"
\"You\'d better not to lie to him, he\'s attentive and he\'s about staying alert!\"
\"I had better not disturb him when he\'s busy with his lessons!\"
The first and the third sentences are incorrect
The second and the fourth sentences are incorrect

The right form is \"I\'d rather (We/You/They\'d better) + not + verb\". There\'s no need for using the preposition \"to\" between \"not\" and a verb. Therefore, the first and the third sentences are incorrect.
PHRASAL VERBS: please, fill in the gap in the sentence:\n\"Do you have an idea why I pulled you __?\"
\"To pull over\" is a phrasal verb that means \"to stop\" (a car). For example: \"Pull over here please.\"
PREPOSITIONS: Complete the following dialogue: \"- Are Lucy and John siblings? Really?\"
Yes, but Lucy is very different to her brother. She\'s kinder.
Yes, but Lucy is very different from her brother. She\'s kinder.

1) \"To be different FROM sth/sb\" = \"to be different TO sth/sb\";\n2) In American English, it is also common to say \"different THAN\": \"Yes, but Lucy is very different THAN her brother. She\'s kinder.\"
IDIOMS: Choose the wrong sentence, if any.
I\'m here to expand my horizons
I\'m here to widen my horizons
I\'m here to broaden my horizons
To expand/widen/broaden someone\'s horizons (idiom) means to increase the range of things someone knows about or has experienced. Therefore, all the sentences are correct.
Do the \"to eat out\" and \"to pig out\" phrasal verbs mean the same?
These phrasal verbs do not mean the same thing because the \"to eat out\" phrasal verb means \"to eat away from home\" and the \"to pig out\" one means \"to eat too much\".
The correct answer is \"injured; damaged.\" \"Injured\" is used when referring to harm to people, while \"damaged\" is used for harm to things or objects such as buildings.
GRAMMAR: please, choose the correct sentence
\"I don\'t want to tell you my name because I keep myself anonymous\"
\"I don\'t want to tell you my name because I keep myself in anonymous\"
\"This line is so long! I can\'t stand waiting in long ones!\"
The first and the third sentences are correct
The second and the fourth sentences are correct
The first and the fourth sentences are correct
The first and the fourth sentences are correct because \"anonymous\" is an adjective; \"can\'t stand/bear + verb + ing\" is a correct form according to grammar.
IDIOMS: I can do this for hours on ___.\nI listen to music for hours on ___.
For hours/days on end - for hours/days without stopping (часами/днями напролёт, без конца).
I was reading a book when my wife called me
I was reading a book for two hours when my wife called me
I had been reading a book for two hours when my wife called me
1) The first action is longer; the second one is shorter.\n2) Because we have \"FOR + some period of time\" (for TWO HOURS), we use the Past Perfect Continuous in that case, not the Past Continuous.
I had no appetite. I could only eat ___.

We use half or half of mostly before a noun with a determiner. We do not normally put a/an or the before half in this case:\nShe spends half (of) her time travelling.\nI gave him half (of) a cheese pie.
This is the ___ film she\'s ever seen.
Let\'s cut ___ the field. This way is shorter. It\'ll save our time.
Cut across = to take a shorter way = to go from one side of an area to the other instead of going round it.
When did the journey start?\n\"Lisa and Kevin had already travelled some distance when the sun rose.\"
1) \"Lisa and Kevin HAD already TRAVELLED some distance\" (Past Perfect shows that this action happened before the action in the Past Simple);\n2) \"when the sun ROSE\" (Past Simple).
It appears to me that the kids ____ the library yet because I can hear their voices from the living room.
Fill in the gap.\nThe situation calls ___ decisive actions.
ARTICLES: Please, choose the correct sentence.
These tourists weren\'t used to such severe climate.
My best friend left for US yesterday. I\'ll be missing him a lot!
I can\'t afford that now cuz! I\'ve been going through a lot and I\'m saving for a trip to the Europe.
The first and the third sentences are correct.
The second and the fourth sentences are correct.
The third and the fourth sentences are correct.
The word \"a climate\" is countable, \"the US\" requires \"the,\" \"to be in a hurry\" requires \"a,\" the word \"Europe\" does not require \"the.\"
What\'s the correct transcription of the word \'nightclub\'?\n\"The city is famous for its numerous nightclubs.\"

Please, fill in the gaps in the sentence:\n\"I can\'t afford that stuff at the moment. I gotta scrape ___ on $200 a month and I\'m paying __ my student loan else. So… that\'s why I still live with my parents.\"

\"To scrape by\" is a phrasal verb that means \"to have money for only some basic things you need and to live barely\"; \"to pay down\" is a phrasal verb that means \"to pay part of an amount you have\".
Fill in the gap:\n\"These patients need ___. Please talk to Mr. Smith about it. I hope he will be able to organise it.\"
1) rehabilitation (uncountable noun) [rɪˌhæblɪˈteɪʃən];\n2) organise - UK; organize - US
Please, fill in the gap in the sentence:\n\"These guys are just liars! Don\'t get taken __ by their false promises and stay away from them!\"
\"To take in\" is a phrasal verb that means \"to deceive\"
What does the chat\'s \"jk\" abbreviation mean?
Choose the correct option:\n\"- Oh, I\'ve left my pen at home. Martin, please throw a pen ___ me.\"

1) We say \'throw something TO somebody/throw sb sth\' when we want to pass sth; 2) We say \'throw sth AT sb\' when we want to do harm: \"Lisa was angry with Jack. That\'s why she threw a plate AT him.\"
He threw that towel to me
He threw that towel at me
1) throw - threw - thrown; 2) \'to throw somebody something\' and \'to throw sth TO sb\' are used when we want to pass something; 3) \'to throw sth AT sb\' is used when we want to do harm.
Do the words \'terrific\' and \'disgusting\' mean the same thing?

The word \'terrific\' means \"wonderful\", \"excellent\", \"marvelous\", and so on; the word \'disgusting\' means \"awful\", \"horrible\", \"dreadful\", and so on. Therefore, these words do not mean the same thing.
Use the past simple (not the present perfect) for things that are not recent or new. Example: Mozart was a composer. He wrote more than 600 pieces of music. My mother grew up in Italy.
Complete the dialogue:\n\"- You can ask Selena for help. - No, I can\'t rely ___ her because she let me down many times.\"

1) In general, these two mean the same thing, but \"to rely UPON someone/something\" is more formal and less common than \"to rely ON someone/something\".\n2) To let someone down (let - let - let) means to disappoint someone by not doing what was expected.
By the time my dad came home, I did my homework
I have done my homework by the time my dad came home
I had done my homework by the time my dad came back home
I did my homework by the time my dad came back home
By the time my dad came home, I had done my homework
By the time my dad came back home, I have done my homework
The first and the fourth sentences are correct
The second and the sixth sentences are correct
The third and the fifth sentences are correct
The Past Perfect tense is used in this case. Therefore, we need to use \"had\" if there is the Past Simple one.
